title: No pretended worship and no likeness of God
source_text: Καὶ οὐ μόνον τὸ εὔχεσθαι „τοῖς ἀγάλμασιν“ ἠλίθιόν ἐστιν ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τὸ συμπεριφερόμενον τοῖς πολλοῖς προσποιεῖσθαι „τοῖς ἀγάλμασιν“ εὔχεσθαι, ὁποῖον ποιοῦσιν οἱ τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ Περιπάτου φιλοσοφοῦντες καὶ οἱ τὰ Ἐπικούρου ἢ Δημοκρίτου ἀσπαζόμενοι· οὐδὲν γὰρ νόθον χρὴ ἐνυπάρχειν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ ἀληθῶς εἰς τὸ θεῖον εὐσεβοῦς. οὐ τιμῶμεν δὲ τὰ ἀγάλματα καὶ διὰ τὸ μὴ τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν καταπίπτειν εἰς ὑπόληψιν τὴν περὶ τοῦ εἶναι τὰ ἀγάλματα θεοὺς ἑτέρους. διὸ καὶ ἐγκαλοῦμεν Κέλσῳ καὶ πᾶσι τοῖς ὁμολογοῦσι μὴ εἶναι ταῦτα θεοὺς ὅτι τῶν δοκούντων εἶναι σοφῶν καὶ ἡ φαινομένη περὶ τὰ ἀγάλματα τιμή· ᾗ καὶ ἀκολουθοῦντες οἱ πολλοὶ οὐ μόνον κατὰ συμπεριφορὰν σέβειν αὐτὰ νομίζοντες ἁμαρτάνουσιν ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ καταπίπτοντες τῇ ψυχῇ ἐπὶ τὸ νομίζειν ταῦτα εἶναι θεοὺς καὶ μηδ᾿ ἀνεχόμενοι ἀκούειν ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶ ταῦτα θεοὶ τὰ ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν προσκυνούμενα. Κέλσος μὲν οὖν φησιν αὐτὰ μὴ ἡγεῖσθαι θεοὺς ἀλλὰ θεῶν ἀναθήματα, μὴ ἀποδεικνὺς. πῶς οὐκ ἀνθρώπων εἰσὶ ταῦτα ἀναθήματα ἀλλ᾿, ὡς ὠνόμασεν, αὐτῶν τῶν θεῶν. σαφὲς γὰρ ὅτι ἐστὶν ἀνθρώπων πεπλανημένων περὶ τὸ θεῖον ταῦτα ἀναθήματα. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ θείας εἰκόνας ὑπολαμβάνομεν εἶναι τὰ ἀγάλματα, ἅτε μορφὴν ἀοράτου καὶ ἀσωμάτου μὴ διαγράφοντες θεοῦ. ἐπεὶ δὲ ὑπολαμβάνει ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος τοῖς ἐναντίοις περιπίπτειν, ὅτε φαμὲν μὴ εἶναι ἀνθρωπόμορφον τὸ θεῖον καὶ ὅτε πιστεύομεν ὅτι „ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησε τὸν ἄνθρωπον“ ἰδίαν „εἰκόνα“ καὶ ἐν εἰκόνι θεοῦ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν· λεκτέον, ὡς καὶ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἴρηται, ὅτι τὸ „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα θεοῦ“ ἐν ψυχῇ λογικῇ, τῇ ποιᾷ κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν, σῴζεσθαί φαμεν. καὶ ἔνθα μέντοι ὁ Κέλσος, μὴ ἰδὼν διαφορὰν εἰκόνος θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα θεοῦ,“ φησὶν ἡμᾶς λέγειν ὅτι „ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησε τὸν ἄνθρωπον“ ἰδίαν „εἰκόνα“ καὶ εἶδος ὅμοιον ἑαυτῷ· εἴρηται δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω καὶ πρὸς ταῦτα.
pass_a_gloss: And not only is praying 'to the images' foolish (ἠλίθιος), but indeed also, going along with (συμπεριφέρομαι) the many (οἱ πολλοί), pretending (προσποιέομαι) to pray 'to the images', of which sort those do who philosophise the things from the Peripatos (Περίπατος) and those embracing (ἀσπάζομαι) the things of Epicurus or Democritus; for nothing spurious/counterfeit (νόθον) ought to be present (ἐνυπάρχω) in the soul (ψυχή) of the one truly (ἀληθῶς) pious (εὐσεβής) toward the divine. And we do not honour the images also on account of not falling, as far as in us lies (τὸ ὅσον ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν), into the supposition (ὑπόληψις) that the images are other gods. Therefore (διό) we also accuse (ἐγκαλέω) Celsus and all those confessing (ὁμολογέω) these not to be gods, that of those seeming (δοκέω) to be wise (σοφοί) is even the apparent (φαινομένη) honour (τιμή) concerning the images; which the many also following (ἀκολουθέω) not only sin (ἁμαρτάνω), thinking (νομίζω) they revere them according to accommodation (συμπεριφορά), but indeed also falling down (καταπίπτω) in soul to thinking these to be gods and not even enduring (ἀνέχομαι) to hear that these things worshipped (προσκυνέω) by them are not gods. Celsus then says they do not consider (ἡγέομαι) them gods but offerings/dedications (ἀναθήματα) of gods, not demonstrating (ἀποδείκνυμι) how these are not offerings of men but, as he named, of the gods themselves. For it is clear that these are offerings of men led astray (πλανάω) concerning the divine. But neither do we suppose (ὑπολαμβάνω) the images to be divine images/likenesses (εἰκόνες), inasmuch as not delineating (διαγράφω) a form (μορφή) of the invisible (ἀόρατος) and incorporeal (ἀσώματος) God. And since Celsus supposes us to fall into (περιπίπτω) contraries (τὰ ἐναντία) when we say the divine is not human-formed (ἀνθρωπόμορφος) and when we believe that 'God made man' [as his] own 'image' and in the image of God made him, it must be said, as was said also above, that we say the 'according to the image (κατ᾿ εἰκόνα) of God' is preserved (σῴζω) in the rational (λογική) soul, the one qualified (ποιά) according to virtue (ἀρετή). And there indeed Celsus, not seeing the difference (διαφορά) of an image of God and of the 'according to the image of God', says that we say that 'God made man' [as his] own 'image' and form (εἶδος) like (ὅμοιος) himself; but it has been said in the things above in reply to these too.
pass_b_english: Not only is it foolish to pray “to images”; it is foolish also to go along with the multitude and pretend to pray “to images”, as those do who follow the philosophy of the Peripatetics, and those who embrace the views of Epicurus or Democritus. For nothing counterfeit should dwell in the soul of one who is truly devout toward the divine. We do not honour images for this reason also: so that, as far as it depends on us, we may not sink into the notion that the images are other gods. That is why we also find fault with Celsus and with all who admit that these are not gods: because those who are reputed to be wise give even the outward show of honour to images. The multitude follow that show, and they not only sin, supposing that they worship the images by way of accommodation, but even sink in their souls into thinking that these are gods, and cannot bear even to hear that the things they bow down to are not gods.

Celsus, then, says that these are regarded not as gods but as the gods’ votive offerings; but he does not show how they are not men’s offerings rather than, as he named them, offerings of the gods themselves. For it is clear that these are the offerings of men who have gone astray about the divine. Nor do we suppose that the images are divine likenesses, since we do not sketch a form of the invisible and bodiless God.

Celsus supposes that we contradict ourselves when we say that the divine is not of human form and yet believe that “God made man” his own “image”, and made him in the image of God (Genesis 1:27; 9:6). To this we must say, as was said also earlier, that we hold that what is “according to the image of God” (Genesis 1:27) is preserved in the rational soul that is shaped by virtue. Here, indeed, Celsus, not seeing the difference between the image of God and what is “according to the image of God”, says that we say “God made man” his own “image” and a form like himself. But this too has been answered earlier.

choices.choice: οἱ τὰ ἀπὸ τοῦ Περιπάτου φιλοσοφοῦντες: ‘those who follow the philosophy of the Peripatetics’ (Aristotle’s school). ἐγκαλοῦμεν ... ὅτι τῶν δοκούντων εἶναι σοφῶν καὶ ἡ φαινομένη περὶ τὰ ἀγάλματα τιμή is elliptic (‘that even the apparent honour of images is [the practice] of those reputed wise’); rendered ‘because those who are reputed to be wise give even the outward show of honour to images’. κατὰ συμπεριφοράν: ‘by way of accommodation’, that is, conforming outwardly to others. ἀναθήματα θεῶν: Celsus’s phrase from 7.62; the genitive can mean offerings made to gods or offerings belonging to gods, and Origen turns it: they are offerings of men. Rendered ‘the gods’ votive offerings’ so the turn can be seen. Genesis 1:27: Origen mixes the LXX wording (κατ᾿ εἰκόνα θεοῦ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν) with ἐν εἰκόνι θεοῦ (as in Genesis 9:6 LXX, ὅτι ἐν εἰκόνι θεοῦ ἐποίησα τὸν ἄνθρωπον); both verses are cited (cf. Genesis 1:26). Origen’s distinction: the Son is the image of God (cf. Colossians 1:15, not quoted here), while man is made ‘according to the image’; the lowercase ‘image of God’ follows the Greek and is not capitalised to avoid adding an interpretation. ‘Answered earlier’: Origen treated this objection in Book 6 (Celsus’s charge at 6.63) and alludes to it at 7.62; no locus added inline.

'sin in thinking that they worship ... by way of accommodation' -> 'sin, supposing that they worship ... by way of accommodation, but even sink' (the sin is not placed in the thinking; οὐ μόνον ... ἀλλὰ γὰρ καί)
'they do not regard these as gods' -> 'these are regarded not as gods' (μὴ ἡγεῖσθαι has no subject; avoids an unclear 'they')
Genesis citation widened to (Genesis 1:27; 9:6), since ἐν εἰκόνι θεοῦ ἐποίησεν follows Genesis 9:6 LXX; bible_refs and note updated
